newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Liberals slip but still have big lead.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Liberals slip but still have big lead.

text.p: Canada's ruling Liberals have slipped to their lowest popularity level since taking office in 1993 but still maintain a strong lead over their rivals, a poll released on Thursday showed.

The Angus Reid/Southam News poll, taken at the end of March, showed support for the Liberals, which oppose tax cuts for now, falling 5 percentage points since February to 41 percent of decided or "leaning" voters.

Their two rivals who are advocating tax cuts showed gains, the Conservatives to 18 percent from 17 percent and Reform Party to 17 percent -- its highest level in two years -- from 12 percent in February.
"The tax cut, while maybe not an issue right now, has potential," Angus Reid's Darrell Bricker was quoted as saying.
Sixty-seven percent of respondents favored a tax cut either immediately or as soon as the budget was balanced.
Election fever has gripped Canadian politicians, even though Prime Minister Jean Chretien does not have to call elections until October 1998.
He is universally expected to call elections this year, the only real debate being whether it will be in June or possibly October.
Many Liberal strategists have argued in favor of June elections to prevent any further erosion of support, and most commentators also are assuming it will be in June.
But 35 percent of those polled said that would be unacceptable, and this included 33 percent of those who said they were Liberal voters.
Chretien spokesman Peter Donolo dismissed concerns on the timing as peripheral. "Most Canadians don't vote on these issues," he told Reuters.
He said it was natural to go for an election in the fourth year of the mandate, but he would not comment further on a date.

The poll had some encouraging news for each party. Reform regained top spot in the western provinces of Alberta and British Columbia after weak showings early in the year, and narrowed the Liberal lead in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
The once-ruling Conservatives, in no region the top party, were nonetheless now within striking distance -- 31 percent against the Liberals' 40 percent -- in Atlantic Canada.
The separatist Bloc Quebecois widened its lead in Quebec over the Liberals, 44 to 36 percent.

Yet the Liberals continued to hold a commanding lead in the political plum, Ontario, with more than one-third of the seats in the House of Commons. Their margin of support was 53 percent to the Conservatives' 14 and Reform's 12, though in the rural areas its support is usually significantly less.
The survey covered 1,500 Canadians, giving a margin of error for the national sample of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points 19 times out of 20.
